A.explanation: The charge of one electron is the elementary charge $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, which is far smaller than one coulomb.

B.explanation: From $Q = It$, one coulomb is the charge passed when $1 \text{ A}$ flows for $1 \text{ s}$.

C.explanation: This describes the electronvolt, an energy unit equal to $1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$, not the coulomb which is a charge unit.

D.explanation: This is $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ for an electron with $v = 1 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, an energy in joules, not a charge in coulombs.

hints: Notice that options A and B describe electric charge while options C and D describe kinetic energy, so check the unit of the coulomb.
Recall the link between charge $Q$, current $I$ and time $t$ for charge transferred in a circuit: $Q = It$.
Compare one coulomb with the charge of a single electron, $1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, and with the energy name given to an electron moved through one volt.
walkthrough: Identify what is asked: the meaning of $1 \text{ C}$, the SI unit of electric charge $Q$.
State the governing relation for current: $I = Q/t$, so rearranged $Q = It$.
Substitute the unit values: $Q = (1 \text{ A})(1 \text{ s}) = 1 \text{ A s} = 1 \text{ C}$.
Check the distractors: one electron carries only $1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, and an electron through $1 \text{ V}$ defines the electronvolt energy, not the coulomb.
Therefore the coulomb is the charge transferred by one ampere in one second. This is option B.
